More trouble for Bisleri as FSSAI sanctions second prosecution over coliform in Bengal plant sample

The action follows a similar case announced by the regulator earlier in the week, involving a water sample from the company's Goa plant that also failed laboratory testing.

Sneha Richhariya

28 November, 2026 11:45 am IST

New Delhi: Bisleri International is facing a second prosecution by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), this time after a packaged drinking water sample from its West Bengal plant tested positive for coliform bacteria, sources told ThePrint Friday. Both the primary and referral laboratories confirmed the finding.

The sample was collected in July this year from the company’s plant in Telipara village, Jalpaiguri district. It belonged to batch PB 201, manufactured on 20 July, 2026 and marked for use by 19 January, 2027. FSSAI prohibited the sale of the batch on 12 August, and has now sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International Pvt Ltd, the sources said.

“It is confirmed that coliform was found in both the primary and the referral tests. Coliform makes the water unsafe,” a source told ThePrint. The source confirmed the details, but said they would not be issued as an official regulator statement for now.

Show Full Article

This is the second time in a single week that FSSAI has sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International Pvt Ltd, a leading player in the packaged drinking water sector in the country.

The action follows a similar case announced by the regulator Sunday, involving a sample from the company’s Goa plant that also failed laboratory testing.

ThePrint has reached out to Bisleri International for a response to the findings and prosecution. This report will be updated when a response is received.

Coliforms are a group of bacteria commonly used as indicators of contamination. While not all coliform bacteria are harmful, their presence in packaged drinking water can point to contamination or lapses in treatment, bottling or handling.

Contamination can occur through source water, inadequate disinfection, unclean bottling equipment, bottles or caps, storage tanks, or leaks in water and sewage systems.

The presence of coliforms does not establish that disease-causing organisms are present. However, contaminated water can carry pathogens that cause illnesses, such as diarrhoea, vomiting, abdominal cramps and fever, for children, older people and those with weakened immunity at greater risk. No illness linked to the batch has been reported so far.

Second case in a week The latest action comes days after FSSAI announced prosecution over a sample from Bisleri’s Goa facility, collected on 30 September, 2025. That sample was declared unsafe under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 for exceeding prescribed bromate limits. After Bisleri appealed, a referral laboratory also declared it unsafe, citing polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), according to the regulator.

Bisleri has disputed the Goa findings, saying its water is safe. It said the matter concerned one batch from 14 months ago at one of its 143 plants. The company said an independent test at an FSSAI-approved laboratory had found bromate levels within permissible limits, and that it had not received the prosecution notice. It said it would cooperate with FSSAI.

On Monday, Bisleri International reiterated that its products were safe for consumption and said it would cooperate with the regulator.

Nationwide sampling The cases come amid a wider surveillance exercise covering packaged water brands, large and small, across the country. Sampling, which has been under way for several months and was recently stepped up, is being carried out mainly by state food safety authorities, alongside FSSAI offices, sources told ThePrint.

FSSAI CEO Rajit Punhani told news agency ANI that laboratory results would take “at least a month or two”, and that there was “no particular reason” for the focus on water. He said the regulator was earlier focusing on dairy, meat, eggs, cereals, energy drinks and sugary drinks.

Punhani said the enforcement exercise was aimed at ensuring compliance with food safety norms, and not creating panic. The regulator is also preparing to inspect packaging materials used for food products.

FSSAI has also asked state food commissioners and regional directors to intensify surveillance, inspections and sampling of packaged and mineral water, and take action against violators. This year, it has stepped up enforcement against food businesses, e-commerce companies, and manufacturers of energy drinks and alcoholic beverages.

Taiwan votes in local elections as China sends warplanes, lambastes Taipei candidate

Reuters

28 November, 2026 09:00 am IST

Follow Us:

By Ben Blanchard and Yimou Lee

TAIPEI, Nov 28 (Reuters) – Taiwan voted for mayors and county chiefs on Saturday in an election dominated by local issues as China surged warplanes around the island and its state media issued a string of rebukes against the ruling party’s Taipei candidate.

Campaigning in the races in all of Taiwan’s 22 cities and counties focused on such issues as transport and the environment. But while the results, expected early in the evening, will not directly affect China policy, Beijing has repeatedly weighed in and continued its military pressure.

Show Full Article

China views Taiwan as its own territory and has denounced Puma Shen, the governing Democratic Progressive Party’s candidate in the key election for mayor of the capital Taipei.

Shen is wanted by Chinese police for “separatism”. He told Reuters this month that police there had never contacted him and that whoever wins, the Taipei election would be a victory for democracy in the face of pressure from China.

On Friday, Chinese state media launched a new wave of attacks against Shen, accusing him of taking money from the United States and saying the US was “using extremely covert methods to deeply interfere” in the vote.

Shen’s team said it could not comment before polls close at 4 p.m. (0800 GMT).

Speaking to reporters after voting, Shen did not mention China, instead talking about how he had slept, what he would have for breakfast and the good weather.

Shen’s main opponent is Mayor Chiang Wan-an from the main opposition party, the Kuomintang (KMT) . His team declined to comment on the Chinese state media reports.

Taiwan’s defence ministry reported on Saturday morning that it had detected 33 military aircraft encircling the island, along with eight Chinese warships, in the previous 24 hours.

China’s Taiwan Affairs Office and the US State Department did not respond to requests for comment outside office hours.

Alex Huang, an adviser to Taiwan’s National Security Council, said China had mobilised its propaganda platforms and the Taiwan Affairs Office on Friday night, marking its own “election eve”.

FOCUS TO SHIFT TO 2028 ELECTION

At the last local elections four years ago, the KMT thrashed the DPP, winning 14 cities and counties to 5 for the DPP. Other parties or independents won the other 3.

Manoeuvring for presidential and parliamentary elections, to be held early in 2028, will begin in earnest after Saturday’s vote.

While President Lai Ching-te will almost certainly stand for a second term, the maximum allowed under the constitution, the KMT has not confirmed its candidate. Its likely frontrunner is former journalist Lu Shiow-yen, mayor of the central city of Taichung.

The KMT traditionally favours close ties with Beijing, whose government refuses to talk to Lai, labelling him a “separatist”. Lai says only Taiwan’s people can decide their future.

Both parties concentrated their efforts on Taipei and the five other biggest cities.

The main race to watch is for the Taipei mayorship, where Chiang has faced a stiff challenge from Shen, an academic-turned-lawmaker and an expert on China’s information warfare.

Other key races are in New Taipei, Taiwan’s most populous city, now held by the KMT, and the traditional DPP stronghold Kaohsiung in the south, where the KMT has campaigned hard.

(Reporting by Ben Blanchard and Yimou Lee; Editing by William Mallard)

By Paolo Laudani and Alvaro Murillo

Nov 27 (Reuters) – Costa Rica denied entry to the United Nations special rapporteur on the Israeli-occupied Palestinian territories, drawing criticism from UN human rights chief Volker Turk on Friday.

Costa Rica’s move put the small Central American country’s increasingly close alignment with Washington and Israel on security and foreign policy into the spotlight.

Show Full Article

Turk said he was “deeply concerned” by Costa Rica’s decision to bar Francesca Albanese from entering the country and urged authorities to reconsider after she was stopped at Juan Santamaria airport, which serves the capital San Jose.

Albanese, an Italian national, had traveled to Costa Rica to receive an honorary doctorate from the state-run University of Costa Rica. A UN special rapporteur is an independent expert appointed by the UN Human Rights Council to investigate and report on rights abuses in a specific country.

The UN human rights office said on X that Albanese was denied entry on “claimed national security grounds.” Costa Rica’s migration office said it had acted after receiving an alert and that the decision was consistent with national security measures.

On Friday evening, Costa Rican authorities allowed Albanese to be transferred to a hotel near the San Jose airport to spend the night before she travels to Mexico on Saturday.

Costa Rica, under President Laura Fernandez, has deepened cooperation with the United States on security and has moved closer to Israel, a notable shift for a country long associated with support for multilateral institutions.

Albanese, who has been sanctioned by the United States under measures related to the International Criminal Court, said she hoped Costa Rica would reverse the decision and rejected what she described as efforts to link her to terrorism.

In a video call interview with journalist Ahmed Shihab-Eldin recorded from a gate at the airport, Albanese said authorities took her passport and that she was offered a detention room to sleep in that was so smelly she almost became ill.

“I was almost forced to board the plane to be shipped back to Paris. I said no, and I opposed it … and they threatened to put me on the plane by force,” she said.

Albanese has become one of the most outspoken international critics of Israel’s conduct in Gaza, making her a frequent target of pro-Israel officials and governments. Israel’s UN ambassador, Danny Danon, praised Costa Rica’s decision in a post on X.

(Reporting by Paolo Laudani and Alvaro Murillo; Editing by Kylie Madry, Rod Nickel and Tom Hogue)

TAIPEI, Nov 28 (Reuters) – Taiwan’s voters were choosing mayors and county chiefs on Saturday in an election that will gauge party support ahead of the island’s 2028 presidential vote, with China paying close attention despite not figuring as a major campaign issue.

Polls close at 4 p.m. (0800 GMT), with results expected in the early evening.

Beijing, which claims Taiwan as its own territory, has ramped up pressure on Taiwan to accept its sovereignty claims, which Taipei rejects.

Taiwan’s Defense Ministry said on Friday it had detected 30 Chinese military aircraft operating around the island, 26 of which crossed the Taiwan Strait’s median line, carrying out a “joint combat readiness patrol” with warships.

China’s Defense Ministry did not respond to a request for comment. It said on Thursday that “reunification” is an unstoppable trend and that Taiwan’s people could feel safer with a “heroic people’s army to protect them”.

At the last local elections four years ago, the Kuomintang thrashed the DPP, winning 14 cities and counties to 5 for the DPP. Other parties or independents won the other 3.

The KMT traditionally favours close ties with Beijing, whose government refuses to talk to Lai, labelling him a “separatist”. Lai says only Taiwan’s people can decide their future.

Both parties concentrated their efforts on Taipei and the five other biggest cities.

The main race to watch is for the Taipei mayorship, where the incumbent Chiang Wan-an from the KMT has faced a stiff challenge from Shen, an academic-turned-lawmaker and an expert on China’s information warfare.

Other key races are in New Taipei, Taiwan’s most populous city, now held by the KMT, and the traditional DPP stronghold Kaohsiung in the south, where the KMT has campaigned hard.
